rv.q: What 'Motown The Musical' lacks in dramatic sophistication, it makes up for with an exuberant celebration of the Motown sound that defined an era.
Here’s what a $150 orchestra seat gets you at “Motown: The Musical”: bargain-basement sets, basic choreography performed merely adequately, and laughable dialogue.
With its narrowly self-serving perspective and simplistic connect-the-dots plotting, Berry Gordy's book makes Jersey Boys look like Eugene O'Neill.
The songs are staggering, the book utterly flimsy.
But some of the scenes, not the least of which is a moment when Gordy chronicles his sexual failings with Ross (a flaw! a flaw!) are laughably bad.
Although reasonably entertaining, it’s unfortunate that “Motown: The Musical” doesn’t quite do justice to Motown, the music, or to its founder.
This show is less a musical than a gilded jukebox, a parade of more than 50 Motown hits performed with an energy that would make the Energizer Bunny collapse from exhaustion.
Rarely has a Broadway musical offered such extremes of talent and inanity.

What saves 'Motown' from being a total washout is its score, which consists of more than 50 songs from the Motown catalog, most of them performed with considerable energy and no small amount of skill.
The restlessness of the story eventually does everyone in, and the direction manages to highlight the script’s deficiencies instead of disguising them.
Maybe the best bad musical ever.
If you prefer a well-written story with multidimensional characters that digs beneath the surface and uses song with dramatic acumen, then steer clear.
It's all too much (in fact, the scene where we learn JFK has been assassinated gets an unwanted giggle), but the script moves better in Act Two, with less jokiness getting in the way of the motion.
When all is sung and done, the show is about imitation more than illumination.
Thanks to a spectacularly talented cast, efficient direction by Charles Randolph
Still, if you can get through the spoken part, Motown offers the best musical nostalgia trip in town.
The only thing hot in 'Motown' is the music.
There simply is no resisting the powerfully familiar music that rocks the rafters of the Lunt-Fontanne Theater.

cn.t: Critics find Motown The Musical dramatically weak but musically irresistible, with Berry Gordy's self-serving book undermining 60+ classic hits performed by a talented cast.

sg.ra: Per SeatPlan and Headout, center rows D-J are the Lunt-Fontanne sweet spot because the house stage sits unusually high and is not raked — patrons halfway back in orchestra report they cannot see the stage floor, so anchoring forward of the overhang line (row W) but back from rows A-C keeps the stage floor visible.

Front Mezz is only 5 rows deep (A-E) with no balcony above, so every row has clean sightlines — and row B specifically beats row A because a safety railing in front of row A cuts into the stage (one source cites ~35% obstruction for some seats), making B the preferred pick that most guides name by row.

SeatPlan and forum posts flag that the mezzanine overhang starts at row J but begins cutting into the top of the stage from row W back across Left, Center, and Right Orchestra — combined with the Lunt-Fontanne's high unraked stage (floor already hard to see from mid-orchestra), rear orchestra loses both the top and bottom of the picture.

The Lunt-Fontanne has no balcony, so unlike most large Nederlander houses the Rear Mezz has zero overhang — SeatPlan specifically names rows B-C as best because they clear the railing behind the Front Mezz that can obstruct row A, and the section's rake keeps sightlines clean despite being the cheapest seats in the venue.

Multiple guides flag that the Lunt-Fontanne's unusually high, non-raked stage makes rows A-C worse than typical Broadway front rows — Headout and TickPick-linked guides warn sightlines can be obstructed because the stage is raised, and any tall patron in front blocks center-stage action at this proximity.
